newsitem.title: SWEDEN: SWEDISH ICE HOCKEY TEAM EAGER TO SKATE ONTO BOURSE.
newsitem.headline: SWEDISH ICE HOCKEY TEAM EAGER TO SKATE ONTO BOURSE.

text.p: Sweden may register its first bourse listing for a sports club this year, with Stockholm ice hockey team Djurgarden announcing proposals on Thursday for a stock market launch.
The Djurgarden sports association hopes to list its ice hockey team on the Stockholm Stock Exchange's O-list for smaller companies in the autumn. Other clubs could follow suit.
The team, established in the early 1920s, has won 14 Swedish championships. It came home with a gold medal from the 1991 European championships and took silver in 1992.

The sports association will present at its June 4 annual meeting plans to spin off its first team and its commercial operations, creating the company Djurgardens IF Hockey AB. This would pave the way for share trading.
It has appointed Enskilda Securities as advisor.

"A listing of Djurgardens IF Hockey AB aims to broaden ownership and...give the company access to capital for the investments necessary to ensure high sports quality, international competitiveness and good profitability," the association said.
Money would be welcome as the association currently has a debt of about 7.5 million crowns ($972,000) but the association said it intended to maintain a strong influence in the listed company.
Shares in sports clubs have become a success overseas with 15 British soccer clubs now listed on the stock market. Aston Villa on Thursday launched its bid for a listing.
The trend has spread overseas with, for example, Zambian football club Mufulira Wanderers considering listing on the Lusaka Stock Exchange later this year.
Djurgarden would be the front runner in Sweden if it made it to the bourse and other sports clubs are likely to follow.
Rival ice hockey team Leksand, based 250 kilometres ( 150 miles) northwest of Stockholm, is also on the starting blocks.

Leksand has previously announced it is interested in seeking a listing and is awaiting approval from the Swedish Sports Federation, which requires a club to be non-profit-making to compete in a Federation league.
"We are working on a listing," Bjorn Doverskog, chairman of the Leksand sports association, told Reuters.
"We hope to be able to transfer our top team to our commercial company and to list it as soon as possible. It'd be good to time it to coincide with the start of the season in September."
Djurgarden and Leksand are looking at ways to bypass the Sports Federation rules.

Leksand intends its non-profit association to lease the players from the commercial listed company to comply with current rules while Djurgarden said its players would represent the non-profit association.

Furthermore, the Alliance group of athletic clubs in Stockholm, comprising Djurgarden's football and hockey teams, Hammarby football and AIK, have submitted a motion to the Sports Federation to change the by-laws.
Doverskog said interest in a Leksand listing was huge.
"I've had 10 companies calling me today alone, asking about our listing," he said.
"Some just think it would be fun to hold a share in Leksand, while other Leksand fans are willing to invest quite a substantial amount of money."
